14250: To scrawl means to write something in a messy, careless way that is hard to read.

When you write neatly, every letter is clear and deliberate. When you scrawl, you write quickly or carelessly — the letters come out uneven, shaky, or tangled together, and someone looking at it might struggle to make out what it says.

Think of a doctor writing a prescription by hand. The letters might be loopy, cramped, overlapping, or wildly uneven. That's a classic example of scrawling. The writing communicates something, but it takes effort (or guessing) to figure out what.

Three things usually go together when someone scrawls:

Speed — Scrawling is almost always rushed. You're not sitting down to write carefully; you're getting something down fast.

Messiness — The result looks untidy. Letters may be irregular in size, poorly formed, or connected in strange ways.

Difficulty to read — This is the most important quality. Scrawled writing isn't just imperfect — it's hard to decipher. If a stranger looked at it, they might not be able to read it easily, or at all.

If only one or two of these are present, you might just say someone wrote messily. When all three come together, that's scrawling.
What It Says About the Writer

Scrawl carries a slightly negative feeling. It quietly suggests one of two things about the person writing: either they were in too much of a hurry to care about neatness, or they simply lack the habit of writing clearly. It's not a harsh insult, but it does suggest a lack of care or control in that moment.

For example, saying "she wrote her number on a napkin" is neutral. Saying "she scrawled her number on a napkin" tells you the writing was hasty and probably barely legible.

• A student scrawls notes in class while the teacher speaks too fast.
  • Someone scrawls a reminder on a sticky note and sticks it to the fridge.
  • A person scrawls their signature at the bottom of a form without paying attention.
  • Graffiti is scrawled across a wall — large, messy, and done quickly.
  • A coach scrawls a play diagram on a whiteboard during a rushed timeout.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Scrawl is flexible. Here are the main patterns:

Scrawl + something + somewhere:
"She scrawled her name across the top of the page."
"He scrawled the address on the back of a receipt."

Scrawl + down (meaning: to write something down quickly):
"I scrawled down the phone number before I forgot it."

Scrawl + out (meaning: to write something out, usually hastily):
"He scrawled out a quick apology and left it on the table."

Scrawl used passively (when the subject receives the action):
"A warning had been scrawled on the wall in red paint."
"Her name was scrawled at the bottom of the letter."

Scrawl used without an object (focusing on the act itself):
"He scrawled in the margins of every book he owned."
How Scrawl Is Different from Similar Words

Write is completely neutral — it says nothing about the quality or speed of the writing. Scrawl is what writing becomes when it's rushed and illegible.

Scribble is the closest word to scrawl, and they're often used interchangeably. However, there's a subtle difference worth knowing: scribble can also mean making random, meaningless marks (like a toddler scribbling with crayons — not real letters at all). Scrawl almost always refers to actual writing — real words or letters, just done very messily. So scrawling is always an attempt at real writing; scribbling sometimes isn't.

Jot means to write something quickly and briefly (e.g., "I jotted down a note"). Jotting doesn't imply the writing is messy or hard to read — just fast and short. Scrawling goes further: it implies the writing is poorly formed.

Scratch (as in "scratch out a note") is informal and similar in feel to scrawl, but is used less commonly and feels slightly more general.
A Small but Important Note on Degree

Scrawl implies writing that is genuinely difficult to read, not just slightly imperfect. If your handwriting is a little uneven but still clear, most people wouldn't call that scrawling. Scrawling is at the worse end of the spectrum — where reading it requires effort, patience, or guesswork.

Occasionally, yes. Writers sometimes use scrawl in a poetic or imaginative way to describe things that look like messy writing. For example: "Lightning scrawled across the sky" — meaning the lightning bolt looked like a chaotic, jagged line, the way scrawled writing does. This is a creative, descriptive use, not the everyday meaning, but it's worth knowing it exists.
To scrawl means to write something quickly and carelessly, producing messy, barely legible handwriting — as if your hand was moving faster than it should and neatness was the last thing on your mind.
14251:
Scrawny means unpleasantly and unhealthily thin — so thin that the person or animal looks weak, frail, or as if they haven't been eating enough. Think of someone whose bones seem to poke out through their skin, whose arms look like sticks, or whose neck looks too narrow to hold up their head properly. That's scrawny.

It's not just "thin." It's thin in a way that looks wrong — like something is missing, like the body hasn't been properly fed or developed.

This is a negative word. When you call someone or something scrawny, you are not complimenting them. You're describing a kind of thinness that looks pitiful, weak, or even a little sad. It often suggests the person or animal looks underfed, underdeveloped, or in poor health.

If you call a child scrawny, you're saying they look worryingly thin. If you call a chicken scrawny, you're saying it barely has any meat on it. The word always carries that sense of not enough — not enough flesh, not enough muscle, not enough substance.
What Can Be Described as Scrawny?

Scrawny is most often used to describe:

  • People — especially their overall body, or specific parts like arms, legs, and neck.
  • Animals — dogs, cats, birds, livestock, etc.
  • Body parts — "his scrawny little arms," "her scrawny neck."
  • Occasionally, plants or trees — a scrawny tree is one that looks thin, bare, and unhealthy.

Scrawny sits at the stronger, more extreme end of words meaning thin. Here's a simple scale to help you feel where it sits:

Slim → Thin → Skinny → Scrawny

  • Slim — thin in an attractive, healthy way. A compliment.
  • Thin — just a neutral description. No judgment.
  • Skinny — noticeably thin, slightly negative but often just casual/descriptive.
  • Scrawny — thin in a way that looks unhealthy, weak, or pitiful. Clearly negative.

So scrawny is not the harshest word in the English language, but it is genuinely unkind. You wouldn't use it to describe someone you want to compliment.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat makes it different from scrawny
SlimPositive. Suggests attractiveness.
LeanPositive or neutral. Suggests low fat but with muscle — like an athlete.
SkinnyClose to scrawny, but less harsh. Sometimes used affectionately.
GauntSuggests a dramatic, hollow thinness usually caused by illness, suffering, or old age. More serious and somber than scrawny.
BonyFocuses specifically on bones being visible. Scrawny covers the whole thin+weak impression.

These examples will show you exactly how the word is used naturally:

  • "The scrawny little kitten could barely stand on its own legs."
  • "He used to be a scrawny teenager, but now he's an athlete."
  • "She picked up the scrawny chicken and frowned — there was hardly any meat on it."
  • "After months of poor eating, he looked pale and scrawny."
  • "The old tree in the yard was scrawny and barely had any leaves left."
  • "Don't let those scrawny arms fool you — he's surprisingly strong."

Scrawny is an informal, everyday word. You'd hear it in casual conversation, fiction, informal writing, or in descriptions in newspapers. You wouldn't typically find it in a formal medical report or an academic paper, where a doctor would say "underweight" or "malnourished" instead.

If you ever need to remember this word quickly: Scrawny = unpleasantly thin, weak-looking, and underfed in appearance — a negative way of describing a person, animal, or thing that looks like it desperately needs more food or strength.
14252:
A scream is a loud, sharp, high-pitched cry that comes out of a person's (or animal's) mouth. It is the kind of sound that cuts through the air, grabs your attention immediately, and is very hard to ignore.

Think of it this way: when something startles you badly, your body sometimes reacts before your mind even processes what happened — and a sound bursts out of your throat. That sound is a scream.
What Makes a Scream a Scream?

Not every loud sound is a scream. A scream has specific qualities:

  • It is loud. It is not a whisper, a murmur, or a soft cry. It has real force and volume behind it.
  • It is high-pitched. It tends to be sharp and piercing, not deep and low.
  • It is sudden and intense. It comes from a place of strong feeling — not calm conversation.
  • It is raw. It is uncontrolled and unfiltered. It is the voice stripped of all social politeness.

This is very important to understand because a scream does not belong to just one emotion. Many very intense feelings can produce a scream:

  • Fear — You see a snake. You let out a scream.
  • Pain — You touch something burning hot. A scream escapes you.
  • Shock or surprise — Someone jumps out from behind a door. You scream.
  • Extreme excitement or joy — Fans at a concert, people on a roller coaster, children tearing open birthday presents — they can all scream too. These are screams of delight, not distress.
  • Grief or anguish — Someone hearing terrible news about a loved one might let out a scream of pure heartbreak.
  • Anger — In a moment of overwhelming rage, someone might release a scream.

So a scream is not always a sign of danger. The emotion behind it can range from horror to pure happiness. The context tells you which kind it is.
A Scream vs. a Shout vs. a Cry

These three words are related but different:

  • A shout is loud and intentional. You shout to be heard across a room or to make a point forcefully. It is controlled.
  • A cry is more emotional and can be quiet — it often involves tears. "She cried all night" does not mean she was making loud sounds necessarily.
  • A scream is specifically loud, sharp, high-pitched, and driven by an overwhelming moment. It is usually not planned. It just happens.

Common patterns you will see:

  • Let out a scream — This is the most natural phrase. "She let out a scream when the lights went off."
  • Give a scream — "He gave a scream and dropped the phone." (Less common than "let out," but correct.)
  • Stifle / suppress a scream — When someone tries very hard not to scream. "She stifled a scream so she wouldn't wake the baby."
  • A scream of + emotion — "a scream of terror," "a scream of delight," "a scream of agony." This tells you what the scream is made of.
  • Let out / hear / let loose a scream — all natural, common collocations.

Describing the scream more precisely:

You will often see adjectives used before "scream" to tell you more about its quality:

  • A piercing scream — so sharp and high that it cuts right through you
  • A blood-curdling scream — so terrifying that it seems to freeze your blood (a very vivid, dramatic description)
  • A silent scream — when someone's mouth opens wide in the shape of a scream, but no sound comes out — usually from shock so severe that the voice itself fails
  • A muffled scream — a scream that is blocked or quieted, perhaps by a hand over the mouth
  • A distant scream — a scream heard from far away

The word "scream" can also describe non-human sounds that have the same sharp, piercing quality:

  • "The kettle let out a scream as the water boiled." — The shrieking whistle of a boiling kettle.
  • "The brakes screamed as the car skidded." — Here "screamed" is used as a verb, but you can say "the scream of the brakes" as a noun too.
  • "The scream of a fighter jet overhead made everyone look up." — The sharp roar of an engine.

In all these cases, the word is used because the sound has that same piercing, urgent, attention-grabbing quality of a human scream.

In informal, conversational English, you might hear:

  • "He/she/it is a scream!" — This means the person or thing is extremely funny, hilarious, a great source of laughter. "Your uncle is a scream — I haven't laughed that hard in years." This usage is old-fashioned and mostly British, but you may encounter it in older books or films.

A scream (noun) is a loud, sharp, high-pitched cry produced by an overwhelming feeling — most commonly fear, pain, shock, or intense excitement. It is raw and forceful. It can come from a person, an animal, or even a machine when that machine makes a similarly sharp, piercing sound. The emotion behind it determines whether it is a scream of terror or a scream of joy. The word pairs naturally with verbs like let out, hear, stifle, and suppress, and with adjectives like piercing, blood-curdling, silent, and muffled.
14253: Scree is a collection of loose, broken rock fragments scattered across a steep mountain or cliff face, or piled up at the bottom of one. Think of it as the rubble that nature chips away from rocky mountainsides over time. If you have ever seen a mountain slope covered in a sea of jagged, loose stones — not soil, not sand, but rough, broken chunks of rock — that is scree.

Scree is made up of sharp-edged, angular rock pieces. This is an important detail: unlike the smooth, rounded pebbles you find in a riverbed (which have been worn smooth by flowing water), scree pieces are jagged and rough, because they have simply snapped off from the rock above and fallen. They have not been tumbled or smoothed.

The size of scree can vary quite a lot — it can range from small, gravelly chips (roughly the size of your thumbnail) all the way to pieces as large as a football, or even bigger. Often, a single scree slope will have a mix of sizes all jumbled together.

The color and type of rock depends entirely on the mountain it came from, so scree can be grey, brown, reddish, or almost any rocky color.

Scree forms on steep, rocky terrain — typically on:

  • The slopes of mountains and hills
  • The faces of cliffs
  • The base of rocky valley walls

The most common reason scree forms is a process called freeze-thaw weathering. Here is how it works: water seeps into tiny cracks in the rock. When temperatures drop, that water freezes and expands. This expansion slowly forces the crack wider. Over many years and thousands of freeze-thaw cycles, chunks of rock eventually snap off and tumble down the slope. Wind, rain, and gravity also help. The broken pieces collect over time, and what you get is scree.

Because of this, scree is especially common in mountainous regions where temperatures regularly go above and below freezing — places like the Alps, the Scottish Highlands, the Himalayas, the Rockies, and similar ranges across the world.
The Two Ways the Word Is Used

The word "scree" can refer to two closely related but slightly different things, and both are correct:

  1. The loose rock material itself — the actual broken fragments, thought of as a collective mass. ("The path disappeared under a thick layer of scree.")
  2. The slope covered by that material — the whole hillside or fan-shaped area blanketed in those loose fragments. ("They had to climb a long scree before reaching the summit.")

In everyday use, you will see it used both ways, often interchangeably, and the meaning is always clear from context.
What It Feels Like to Walk On

This is worth knowing, because it helps the word come alive. Walking on scree is notoriously difficult and tiring. Because the rocks are loose and unstable, every step you take causes them to shift and slide beneath your feet. You can feel like you are taking two steps forward and sliding one step back. It requires careful footing and a lot of energy. Experienced hikers and mountaineers treat scree with respect, because a slip on a steep scree slope can be dangerous.

Interestingly, there is a technique called scree running (or scree skiing) that some experienced hillwalkers use to descend a scree slope quickly — essentially letting the loose rocks slide with you in a controlled way as you run downhill. It looks almost like running on a slow-moving conveyor belt of gravel.
The Word as a Mass Noun

Grammatically, "scree" is almost always used as an uncountable (mass) noun — just like "sand" or "mud." You do not say "a scree" or "several screes" (referring to individual rock pieces). Instead, you say:

  • "There was scree everywhere."
  • "The slope was covered in scree."
  • "They crossed a scree field."

You can say "a scree slope" or "a scree field" or "a scree fan" — these are compound noun phrases describing a place or feature defined by scree, and these are countable.

What it isLoose, broken, angular rock fragments on or at the base of a steep rocky slope
WhereMountain and cliff faces, steep rocky hillsides, worldwide
How it formsRock breaks off (mainly through freeze-thaw cycles) and accumulates
Key qualityUnstable and difficult to move across
Word useRefers to the material and/or the slope covered by it

• "The final stretch of the climb involved a grueling trek across loose scree."
  • "Loose scree rattled down the cliff face and landed far below."
  • "The mountain rescue team had difficulty crossing the unstable scree in the dark."
  • "A vast fan of scree spread out below the sheer rock wall."
  • "She planted each foot carefully, knowing the scree could shift at any moment."

After reading this, you know what scree looks like, how it forms, where it appears, how it behaves underfoot, and how the word is used grammatically and in sentences. You are fully equipped to understand it in any book, article, or conversation you encounter it in.
14254:
A screech is a sharp, high-pitched, harsh sound — the kind that is unpleasant to hear and seems to stab right into your ears. Think of the sound when someone drags fingernails across a blackboard, or when a car slams on its brakes suddenly. That jarring, grating, almost metallic shrillness — that is a screech.

It is not soft. It is not low. It is not smooth or musical. A screech is raw, shrill, and abrasive. It almost always causes an involuntary reaction: you wince, you freeze, or you spin around to find the source.
What makes a sound a "screech" specifically?

A screech has three defining qualities working together:

High pitch — It sits at the upper end of the sound range. No deep rumbles or bass tones. It is thin and shrill.

Harshness — It is unpleasant and rough. Not smooth, not musical. It has an abrasive, grating quality that makes the ears uncomfortable.

Sharpness and intensity — It has a cutting, piercing character. It tends to arrive suddenly and forcefully, demanding your attention whether you want to give it or not.

From people:
When a person is suddenly terrified, in pain, or overwhelmed by shock, they may let out a screech. It is the voice going to its highest, most strained and uncontrolled register. Imagine someone walking into a dark room and finding a large spider right in front of their face — that sudden, sharp, involuntary sound tearing out of their throat is a screech.

From animals:
Many animals screech. Owls — particularly the barn owl and the aptly named "screech owl" — produce a piercing, raspy cry that sounds nothing like the classic movie hoot; it is more like a high-pitched, unsettling rasp tearing through the night. Cats locked in a fight screech. Parrots screech. Many wild birds screech. Monkeys screech.

From objects and machines:
Inanimate things screech through friction or force. A car's tires screech when it brakes hard or takes a sharp turn too fast. Metal grinding against metal produces a screech. A rusty gate hinge screeches when it swings. A violin bow drawn badly across the strings can produce a screech. These mechanical screeches have the same essential quality: high, harsh, cutting, and deeply unpleasant.
How is a screech different from similar words?

English has several words for sharp, loud sounds, and they are easy to confuse. Here are the key distinctions:

Screech vs. Scream — A scream is closely related, but it is fuller, deeper, and more sustained. A scream uses the whole voice. A screech is thinner, sharper, and more shrill — almost metallic. You could say a screech is what a scream sounds like when it has been pushed to its highest, most strained pitch. All screeches made by humans are close to screams, but not all screams are screeches.

Screech vs. Shriek — These are very similar, and writers sometimes use them interchangeably. The subtle distinction is that a shriek is more often tied to strong emotion — terror, surprise, or even excitement — while a screech carries a rougher, more abrasive quality, like something being scraped or torn. The screech of a saw cutting through metal; the shriek of someone who just received a terrible shock.

Screech vs. Squeal — A squeal is high-pitched but softer, rounder, and more sustained. Think of an excited child squealing with happiness, or a pig. A squeal can even sound joyful. A screech is more harsh, more forceful, and more unpleasant.

Screech vs. Squeak — A squeak is similar in pitch but much smaller — a mouse, a rubber toy, a slightly sticky door. A screech is far more intense and forceful.

Screech vs. Wail — A wail is long, mournful, and sustained — a siren, or a person crying in grief. It lacks the sharp, cutting quality of a screech.

Screech vs. Howl — A howl is deeper and prolonged. A wolf howls. Completely different from the high, sharp character of a screech.

"Screech" is also used beyond describing a literal sound:

  • It can describe music played very badly, so harshly and gratingly that it wounds the ears: "The screech of that out-of-tune violin was unbearable."
  • It is sometimes used for any sudden, sharp audio disturbance: "The screech of feedback from the microphone silenced the entire audience."
  • In informal writing, any sudden harsh, ear-piercing sound — however it is caused — might loosely be called a screech if it has that shrill, cutting quality.

1. "The screech of the brakes echoed across the empty street as the car stopped just in time."
  2. "A screech from deep in the forest made her grip her flashlight tighter."
  3. "He let out a screech when the cat leaped onto his lap from the dark corner."
  4. "The screech of metal on metal told the engineers the machine was about to break down."
  5. "From the top of the stairs came the screech of her little brother sliding on the wooden floor in his socks."

If you have ever been near a parrot at close range — that raw, piercing, almost painfully high-pitched cry — that is a perfect screech. Or think of the sound effect used in horror films at the exact moment something frightening appears on screen: sudden, shrill, cutting, impossible to ignore. Your brain registers it as a warning signal before you have even had time to think. That involuntary "my ears, my nerves" reaction is precisely what a screech triggers.
14255:
To screech means to make a loud, sharp, high-pitched sound that is harsh and unpleasant to the ear. Think of it as a sound that feels like it stabs through the air — it is not just loud, it is also piercing and grating. It is the kind of sound that makes you flinch, cover your ears, or feel a jolt of discomfort the instant you hear it.

A simple way to picture it: if a scream is a knife, a screech is a serrated knife — rough, jagged, and cutting.

Three qualities must come together for a sound to be called a screech:

1. High-pitched — it sits at the upper, sharp end of sound. It is not a low rumble or a deep boom.

2. Loud — it is not a quiet or gentle sound. It forces itself into your attention.

3. Harsh or grating — this is the most important part. A screech is not just a high, loud sound. It has a rough, unpleasant, almost scratchy quality to it. It is not smooth or musical. It irritates the ears.

All three together = a screech. If a sound is high and loud but still somewhat pleasant, it is probably not a screech.

People

A person screeches when they are in extreme emotional distress — overwhelming fear, sharp pain, or intense rage. It is an involuntary, explosive sound that the body produces when it is pushed to its limits.

  • A child who sees a spider suddenly screech in fright.
  • Someone who burns their hand might screech in pain before they even realize what happened.
  • An angry person might screech at someone during a heated argument — meaning they speak in a sharp, harsh, high-pitched voice that has lost all calm.

Note that when a person screeches, it suggests they are out of control of their voice. It is raw, unfiltered, and extreme.

Animals

Many animals screech naturally, and it is one of the most common uses of the word.

  • Owls are famous for screeching in the dark of the night — a sharp, eerie cry.
  • Parrots, hawks, and other birds screech.
  • Cats screech when they are in a fight or in great pain.
  • Bats screech.
  • Monkeys screech when alarmed.

When used for animals, "screech" does not carry any negative judgment — it simply describes the natural sound they make.

Objects and Machines

This is a very important and common use of the word. Inanimate things can also screech when they produce that same sharp, harsh, grating sound.

  • Car tyres screech when a driver brakes suddenly or takes a sharp turn at speed. The rubber drags across the road and produces that sharp, tearing sound.
  • Brakes screech when they are worn out or applied with great force.
  • A door with rusty or unoiled hinges screeches when you open or close it.
  • Chalk on a blackboard screeches — that universally dreaded sound.
  • Metal scraping against metal screeches.
  • A microphone held too close to a speaker screeches (the feedback sound).

The logic is the same: the object is producing a sound that is sharp, high-pitched, and deeply unpleasant.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Screech" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong sense of unpleasantness and intensity. When you use it, you are signalling that the sound was jarring, disturbing, or at least very hard to ignore.

Compare these two sentences:

  • She made a high-pitched sound.
  • She screeched.

The second sentence is far more vivid. You immediately feel the discomfort of the sound, its sharpness, and the extreme emotional state behind it.

Understanding where "screech" sits among related words will sharpen your feel for it.

Scream — A scream is loud and high-pitched but can be relatively smooth and sustained. Think of a horror movie scream — it is long, clear, and piercing. A screech, by contrast, is harsher and rougher. A screech sounds more broken and jagged than a scream.

Shriek — A shriek is the closest word to screech. Both are sudden, loud, and high-pitched. The difference is subtle: a shriek is often a brief, sharp burst of sound, while a screech tends to have more of that rough, grating, unpleasant quality. You might shriek with surprise or delight; you screech with something more raw and uncomfortable.

Yell — A yell is simply very loud. It does not have to be high-pitched at all. A soldier yells a command; a screech is not a command — it is a reaction.

Wail — A wail is long, sustained, and mournful — think of grief or deep sadness. It rises and falls like a wave. A screech is sharp and sudden, not mournful.

Squeal — A squeal is high-pitched and sharp, often from animals (pigs squeal) or from tyres. It is similar to a screech but generally shorter and slightly less harsh. Squeals can even sound almost excited or playful, especially from children. A screech is always more intense and unpleasant.

To see the word in action across different situations:

  1. The owl screeched from somewhere deep in the dark forest.
  2. She screeched when she opened the door and found the stranger standing there.
  3. The car screeched to a stop just inches from the child.
  4. He was so angry that he began screeching at everyone in the room.
  5. The old gate screeched every time the wind pushed it open.
  6. The children screeched with laughter as they chased each other around the garden. (Here it is used for extreme, uncontrolled excitement — the sound is so intense it crosses into screech territory.)
  7. The brakes screeched in protest as the train tried to slow down.

The heart of "screech" is this: it is not just a loud or high-pitched sound — it is a sound with a rough, sharp, harsh edge that makes it deeply unpleasant and impossible to ignore. Whether it comes from a person, an animal, or a machine, a screech always grabs your attention in the most jarring possible way. It is sound at its most raw, sharp, and uncomfortable.
14256: The word screed has two distinct meanings that exist in completely separate worlds — one in everyday language, and one in the world of building and construction. A learner is far more likely to encounter the first meaning, so we'll give it the most attention.
Meaning 1: A Long, Angry Piece of Writing or Speech

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often, especially in newspapers, books, and online discussions.

A screed is a long, rambling, and usually angry or bitter piece of writing or speech — one that goes on and on, often complaining about something or ranting against someone. The word carries a strong sense of excess — too much emotion, too many words, and not enough restraint.

Think of it this way: if someone has a complaint, a reasonable person states it clearly and stops. But the person writing or delivering a screed keeps going. And going. They pile on accusations, frustrations, and grievances until the whole thing becomes exhausting to read or listen to.

The feeling a screed gives you

When you read a screed, you often feel:

  • Like the writer is venting rather than reasoning
  • Like the piece is one-sided and emotionally driven
  • Slightly overwhelmed by the sheer length and intensity of it

It's not just long — a long academic paper isn't a screed. And it's not just angry — a short, sharp complaint isn't a screed either. A screed is the combination of length + anger/bitterness + a sense of going overboard.

Examples in sentences

  • "He posted a ten-page screed online accusing the company of ruining his life."
  • "Her letter to the editor started as a polite concern but turned into a bitter screed against the entire city council."
  • "Nobody read past the first paragraph of his screed because it was so exhausting."

Words that are close in meaning

Understanding nearby words helps pin down exactly what screed means:

  • A rant is similar, but shorter and more commonly spoken. A rant is over in a minute; a screed tends to be longer and more written.
  • A tirade is a fierce, verbal outburst — loud, dramatic, in-your-face. A screed can be quieter and more calculated, but equally excessive.
  • A diatribe is a bitter, critical piece of writing or speech against a person or thing — very close to screed, but diatribe feels slightly more focused in its attack. A screed can be more chaotic and meandering.
  • A polemic is an aggressive argument against something — but a polemic can be well-structured and even intellectually serious. A screed rarely is.

So if you imagine a dial that goes from "calm, reasoned argument" to "unhinged emotional outpouring," a screed sits firmly toward the unhinged end — but it still has words and sentences, unlike pure shouting.

Important nuance: it's almost always used negatively

When someone calls a piece of writing a screed, they are almost always dismissing it. They're signalling: "Don't take this too seriously — this person has lost their composure." It's a word that discredits the piece it describes. Writers and speakers use it as a weapon to undermine something they disagree with.

However, be aware: sometimes the word is used loosely just to mean any very long, forceful piece of writing, even without full contempt. Context will tell you how harshly it's being used.
Meaning 2: A Construction and Building Term

In the world of flooring, plastering, and construction, screed has a completely different and technical meaning.

What it means

In construction, a screed is a smooth, flat layer of material — usually a mixture of cement and sand — that is applied over a rough concrete floor to create a level, even surface. Think of it as the finishing coat that makes a floor ready to have tiles, wood, or carpet laid on top of it. Before the screed, the floor might be rough and uneven; after the screed, it is flat and solid.

The word is also used for the tool itself — a long, straight-edged board or metal bar that a builder drags across wet concrete or plaster to make it perfectly flat and level. The action of using this tool is called "screeding."

In plastering walls, a screed can also refer to a thin strip or band of plaster applied at intervals on a wall, which acts as a guide — like a ruler mark — to help the plasterer know how thick to apply the rest of the plaster coat.

Examples in sentences

  • "The builders laid a cement screed over the ground floor before fitting the tiles."
  • "The screed needs at least 24 hours to dry before anyone walks on it."
  • "He used a metal screed to level the wet concrete across the entire room."

The connecting thread

At first glance, a long angry speech and a flat layer of cement seem to have nothing in common. But both meanings share a vague sense of something being spread out, drawn out, or extended — whether it's words being stretched on and on across a page, or wet concrete being stretched flat across a floor.

In everyday languageA long, bitter, rambling piece of writing or speech; a rant that goes on excessively
In constructionA flat, levelling layer of cement/sand applied to floors; or the tool used to level it

The first meaning is the one you'll need in almost every real-world context. The second is specialist vocabulary you'll encounter if you ever read about building, renovation, or construction.

If you ever want to check whether you're using screed correctly in the everyday sense, ask yourself: "Is this piece of writing or speech long, angry, and excessive — the kind where the person just can't seem to stop complaining?" If yes — it's a screed.
14257: Before diving into the many meanings, here is a thought that will make everything easier: a screen is almost always something that stands between two things. It might divide, protect, hide, filter, or display — but in every case, it sits in the middle, doing a job because of where it is positioned. Hold onto that idea, and every meaning below will feel natural rather than random.

This is what most people think of first today. A screen is a flat surface on which images, text, or video appear. Your phone has a screen. Your laptop has a screen. A television has a screen at its front. A cinema has a large screen mounted at the front of the room onto which a projector throws moving images.

In each case, the screen sits between the machine and your eyes — it takes information from inside a device and makes it visible to you.

Because of this meaning, "screen" also became shorthand for the world of cinema itself. When people say "the big screen," they mean the movies or cinema. "The silver screen" is an older, more poetic phrase for the same idea. When someone is described as "a star of the screen," it means they are a film actor. The screen, in this sense, refers to the whole experience and industry of cinema, not just the physical surface.
A Panel That Divides or Hides

Long before televisions and computers existed, a screen was a physical panel used to divide a space, create privacy, or block something from view. Picture a tall, folding decorative panel placed in a bedroom so that someone can change their clothes behind it, hidden from the rest of the room. That is a screen.

In old European churches, you will often find a structure called a chancel screen or a rood screen — an ornate partition that separates the main hall where the congregation sits from the altar area where the clergy conduct the service. It is a screen because it creates a boundary between two parts of the space.

This kind of screen does not need to be solid or impenetrable. Its defining job is to separate, divide, or shield — even partially.
A Mesh or Net That Filters

A screen can also be a sheet of fine mesh — wires or threads woven tightly together, leaving tiny holes between them. This kind of screen allows certain things to pass through while blocking others.

Window screens and door screens are the most familiar everyday example. In countries where mosquitoes or flies are common, homes have these fine mesh panels fitted over windows and doors. The holes in the mesh are small enough to stop insects from entering, but open enough to let air flow through freely. You can enjoy a cool breeze without inviting bugs inside.

In cooking, building, mining, and many industries, a screen is used to sort materials by size. Sand, gravel, soil, flour, and countless other materials are passed through screens so that fine particles fall through the holes while larger pieces are caught on top. This separating or sorting action is called screening. You may know a smaller, handheld version of this tool as a sieve — it works on the same principle.

Growing naturally from the idea of a dividing panel, a screen can refer to anything that hides, protects, or conceals — even if it is not a man-made object at all.

"A screen of trees" describes a row of trees planted or growing in a line that blocks the view from one side to the other. The trees function as a natural screen. Similarly, smoke can act as a screen, hiding the movements of soldiers or ships from the enemy. This is where the word "smokescreen" comes from — originally a literal cloud of smoke used in warfare to conceal, and later a figurative term for any deception used to hide the truth.

In military contexts, a screen is a force of soldiers, ships, or aircraft positioned in front of a larger force to protect it, gather information, or prevent the enemy from knowing what lies behind.

In basketball, a screen — also called a "pick" — is a move where one offensive player positions their body to legally block a defending opponent. This creates space so that a teammate can move freely to receive a pass or attempt a shot. The player doing this is said to be "setting a screen." Their body, in that moment, works exactly like a physical screen: it is a barrier placed between two people to block one of them.

In screen printing — a widely used method for printing designs onto T-shirts, posters, and other surfaces — a screen is a fine mesh stretched tightly over a frame. Certain parts of the mesh are blocked with a coating, and other parts are left open. When ink is pressed across the screen, it passes through only the open mesh areas and lands on the surface below, creating the printed design. The blocked areas act as a stencil, and the open mesh areas let the ink through. This is the same filtering logic as a window screen, applied to art and manufacturing.

Every meaning of "screen" comes back to the same core idea: something positioned between two sides, doing a job because of where it stands.

Between a device and your eyes, it displays images. Between two parts of a room, it divides and provides privacy. Between insects and the inside of your home, it filters. Between an army and the enemy, it conceals and protects. Between a basketball player and their defender, it blocks. Between ink and a surface, it controls what passes through.

Once you see this, the word "screen" stops feeling like a list of unrelated meanings and becomes one coherent idea expressed in many different situations.
14258: To understand "screen" as a verb, it helps to think about what physical screens actually do. A cinema screen displays images. A wire mesh screen on a window filters — it lets air in but keeps insects out. A decorative room divider conceals one part of a space from another. The verb "screen" borrows all three of these actions: to show, to filter, and to hide. Every meaning of the verb traces back to one of these three core ideas.
Meaning 1 — To show or broadcast a film or programme

When a film, documentary, or video is "screened," it is shown to an audience — in a cinema, on television, at a festival, or in any viewing setting.

"The director's debut film will be screened at the Cannes Film Festival."
"The documentary was screened on national television last night."

This meaning is straightforward: the film is put onto a screen for people to watch. "Screened" in this sense is interchangeable with "shown" or "broadcast," though it tends to sound slightly more formal and is often used in the context of events or public showings.
Meaning 2 — To examine, test, or check people or things in order to make a decision

This is the most widely used meaning in modern English, and it is the richest one. It comes from the image of a wire mesh sieve — the kind that lets certain particles fall through while holding back others. When you "screen" people or things, you are running them through some kind of test or evaluation to decide who or what passes and who or what does not.

This meaning appears across several important areas of life:

In medicine, to screen someone means to test them for a disease or health condition — usually before any symptoms have appeared — so that problems can be caught early and treated.

"All adults over 50 are encouraged to be screened for colon cancer."
"The clinic screened thousands of people for the virus during the outbreak."

The purpose of medical screening is early detection. It is a proactive test applied to a large group, not a diagnostic test for someone already feeling ill.

In employment, when a company screens applicants, it examines a large pool of candidates and filters them down to a smaller, more suitable group before moving to interviews or further stages.

"The HR department screened over 400 résumés before selecting 12 candidates for interviews."
"She was screened out early because she lacked the required qualifications."

Notice those two phrases — "screened in" and "screened out." To be screened in means you have passed the filter and moved forward in the process. To be screened out means you have been eliminated. These are very useful phrases to know.

In security, authorities screen people and their belongings at airports, courthouses, events, or any controlled area to check for weapons, prohibited items, or threats.

"All passengers must be screened before boarding the aircraft."
"Bags are screened using X-ray machines at the entrance."

For background checks, organisations screen individuals by looking into their past — criminal records, financial history, work references, and so on — before trusting them with a role or responsibility.

"The school screens all staff members before hiring."
"Volunteers who work with children are carefully screened."

In all of these contexts — medical, employment, security, background — the underlying logic is identical: a large, unfiltered group goes in, and a smaller, selected group comes out the other side. Some pass; some do not. That is the essence of this meaning.
Meaning 3 — To hide, shield, or protect something from view or harm

Here the verb draws on the idea of a physical room divider or a row of trees — something that acts as a barrier, blocking a view or protecting something behind it.

"A tall hedge screens the garden from the road." (The hedge hides the garden from people passing by.)
"She raised her hand to screen her eyes from the sun." (Her hand acted as a shield against the light.)
"A line of trees was planted to screen the factory from the surrounding neighbourhood."

In this sense, "screen" is close in meaning to shield, hide, block, or conceal. The key detail is that something — a physical object, a natural barrier, or even a person — is being placed between two things to prevent one from being seen or affected by the other.
Meaning 4 — To separate material by passing it through a mesh (technical)

In construction, engineering, mining, and geology, "to screen" means to pass raw material — gravel, sand, soil, ore — through a physical mesh screen so that particles of different sizes are separated. Smaller particles fall through; larger ones are held back.

"The workers screened the gravel to separate fine sand from larger stones."
"The ore was screened to remove large debris before processing."

This is the most literal and technical meaning, closest to the physical object. You are unlikely to encounter it in everyday conversation, but it is worth knowing.

This is a common everyday phrase that deserves its own explanation. To "screen" a phone call means to check who is calling before deciding whether to pick up — often by letting it ring or go to voicemail so you can assess it first.

"She never answers unknown numbers — she always screens her calls."
"His assistant screens all incoming calls before putting anyone through to him."

The logic here is again the filter: you are deciding which calls get through to you and which do not, rather than accepting every call blindly.

Whenever you see "screen" used as a verb, ask yourself which of these three actions is happening:

Showing → a film or programme is being displayed to an audience.
Filtering → people or things are being examined and sorted — some pass, some do not.
Hiding → something is being placed behind a barrier to block it from view or protect it from harm.

The filtering meaning is by far the most common in modern English. Whether it is a doctor testing patients, a company reviewing job applications, a security guard checking bags, or someone deciding not to pick up a phone call — in each case, there is a process of examination and selection at work, and the word for all of it is "screen."
14259:
To scribble means to write or draw something quickly and carelessly, in a way that looks messy, rushed, or hard to read. It's the opposite of writing neatly and thoughtfully.

Think of it this way: when you write, you're being careful and deliberate. When you scribble, you're doing it fast, without caring much about how it looks.

1. Writing messily or carelessly

This is the most common use. When someone scribbles words or letters, the handwriting is usually difficult to read because the person was either rushing, being lazy about neatness, or not paying attention.

  • He scribbled his signature so fast that it was impossible to recognize.
  • The doctor scribbled something on the prescription, and the pharmacist could barely read it.
  • She scribbled her phone number on a napkin and handed it to him.

Notice that in all these examples, the writing happened fast and the result looks messy or rough.

2. Making random, meaningless marks

When someone — especially a child — makes random lines, squiggles, or shapes on paper with no clear intention, that's also called scribbling. There's no real drawing happening; it's just uncontrolled marks.

  • The toddler grabbed a crayon and scribbled all over the wall.
  • He was bored in the meeting and just scribbled circles on his notepad.

This is important. When you use the word "scribble," you are automatically communicating a few things beyond just the action itself:

  • Speed — it was done quickly, not slowly and carefully.
  • Carelessness — neatness was not a priority.
  • Low importance — it's usually something informal or temporary, not a final, polished piece of writing.
  • Roughness — the result isn't clean or precise.

So if someone says "I scribbled a note and left it on the table," you immediately understand the note was short, written fast, and probably not very neat — all from just that one word.

You'll often see "scribble" used with these patterns:

Scribble + something
→ She scribbled a quick note.
→ He scribbled an address.

Scribble + on/over + something (to mark a surface messily)
→ The kids scribbled on the wall.
→ Someone scribbled over the poster.

Scribble + down + something (to write something quickly so you don't forget it)
→ Let me scribble down your number before I forget.
→ She scribbled down a few ideas during the phone call.

Scribble + in + something (to write inside a specific place, like a notebook or margin)
→ He scribbled notes in the margins of the book.
How It's Different from Similar Words

Scribble vs. Write
"Write" is completely neutral — it just means putting words on paper. "Scribble" always carries the idea of messiness and speed. You can write something neatly; you can never scribble something neatly.

Scribble vs. Jot
"Jot" (as in "jot down") also means to write something quickly. But "jot" doesn't suggest messiness — it just means briefly. "Scribble" goes further, suggesting the result also looks rough.

Scribble vs. Doodle
"Doodle" means drawing small, casual, often creative or patterned drawings (like little stars or faces) while your mind is elsewhere. "Scribble" is more random and purposeless — it's less artistic than doodling, even in a casual sense.
The Overall Feeling of the Word

If you had to give "scribble" a personality, it would be hasty, informal, and a little bit chaotic. It is not a word that suggests elegance, care, or precision. Whenever you hear or read it, picture someone with a pen moving fast across a page, not lifting their wrist properly, not worrying about the result — just getting something down quickly before the moment passes.

That image — fast hand, messy result, low concern for neatness — is scribbling.
